Polish a Break-Point Term's Positions Over Every Interval

Source: R/seg_hold.R
seg_polish_exact.Rd

Minimizes the least-squares profile of a sharp seg(), jump() or jseg() term over the positions of its break-points, one break-point at a time while the others are held. The profile of a jump() or a jseg() is constant between consecutive distinct values of the covariate, and the profile of a seg() has one stationary point inside each such interval. The minimum over one break-point is therefore found interval by interval, and this function does that for every interval inside the confinement limits.

Usage

seg_polish_exact(term, y, sweeps = 10, weights = NULL)

Arguments

term

A built break-point term (see term_build()).

y

A numeric vector of finite values, one per observation of the build data: the response, net of whatever the caller wants to hold fixed.

sweeps

At most how many passes over the positions. Defaults to 10. The descent stops once a full pass moves no position.

weights

Optional non-negative weights, one per observation; the profile is then weighted least squares.

Value

The term at the polished positions (see seg_relocate()), or the term itself when there is no interval inside the confinement limits.

Details

Write \(F\) for the columns that do not move with the break-point that is being polished (an intercept, the covariate where the term carries a linear part, and the columns of the other break-points), and \(a(q)\) for the columns that do: the indicator \(1(x > q)\), and for a jseg() also the truncated line \((x - q)1(x > q)\). The residual sum of squares at \(q\) is that of the response on \(F\) less the part of the remainder that \(a(q)\) explains, and every cross product that involves \(a(q)\) is a sum over the observations above \(q\) of a fixed quantity, or of one fixed quantity minus \(q\) times another. After the observations are sorted once, those sums are cumulative sums, so all the intervals together cost \(O(np^2)\), whereas one linear fit per interval would cost more. The sweeps over the break-points repeat, at most sweeps times, until a sweep leaves every break-point in place. Inside an interval between consecutive distinct values of the covariate, the span of the columns of a jump() or a jseg() does not depend on \(q\), so each break-point of these terms is placed at the midpoint of its interval.

For a seg() the column that moves is \((x - q)_+\). Inside the interval between the consecutive values \(u_k < u_{k+1}\) it is \(t - q s\), with \(s = 1(x > u_k)\) and \(t = x s\), so the part of the residual sum of squares that it removes is \((c_t - q c_s)^2 / (a_{tt} - 2 q a_{ts} + q^2 a_{ss})\), where \(c\) and \(a\) are the cross products of \(t\), \(s\) and the response after the fixed columns are projected out. Its one stationary point is \(q^* = -b/\gamma\) of the least-squares fit on \(t\) and \(s\). The minimum over the interval is at \(q^*\), when that falls inside the interval, or at one of the two ends, whichever gives the smaller residual sum of squares. The ends are consecutive observed values of the covariate or confinement limits.

seg_polish() sweeps instead a grid of k quantiles of the covariate, so that the position that it reaches is accurate only to the resolution of the grid.

The profile is the least-squares fit of y on an intercept and the term's own columns, which is exact for a gaussian response. For any other family, the fitting layer uses the positions that the profile gives only where its own objective improves. The response must be finite, and missing values are rejected.

A held term whose break-point is developed, \(\psi_i = w_i'p\) with \(w_i\) the row of the sub-design, is polished in the coefficients \(p\). Along a line \(p + tv\) the position of observation \(i\) crosses \(x_i\) at \(t_i = (x_i - \psi_i)/(w_i'v)\), so the profile is evaluated once between each pair of consecutive crossings. For a jseg() the profile is then also minimized inside the best interval, where it varies smoothly. Where the sub-design partitions the observations into groups (psi ~ g, by = ~ 0 + g), the lines move the position of one group at a time, which is a search over every interval of that group. The sweep is also started from each group's own minimum, which is the minimum of the profile when only the observations of that group are used, and the better of the two results is kept. Otherwise the lines are the coordinate directions and, in each plane of two coordinates, six further fixed directions, so that the result is the best point found along those lines and not a global minimum. A developed jump() or jseg() is polished only when held (see seg_hold()), and a developed seg() is rejected.

See also

seg_polish(), seg_hold(), seg_profile_rss().

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(300, 0, 10)))
dd$y <- 2 * (dd$x > 3) - 1.5 * (dd$x > 7) + rnorm(300, sd = 0.3)
b <- term_build(jump(x, npsi = 2, psi = c(2, 5)), dd)
seg_psi(seg_polish_exact(b, dd$y))
#> [1] 3.025479 6.975970
